summary: Explains in more depth how to use IPsec to protect signaling between mobile nodes and home agents in Mobile IPv6. It illustrates packet formats, configuration and processing order. It was updated by RFC 4877.

eli5.summary: Messages between a traveling device and its home base must stay secret. This shows exactly how to wrap them.

questions: how is mobile ipv6 protected by ipsec
what is a home agent in mobile ipv6
why use esp for binding updates
what is the alternate care-of address option
subtitle: Exactly which headers, policies and key exchanges protect a roaming IPv6 device's conversations with its home agent.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 needs IPsec to protect signaling between a mobile node and its home agent, but the base specification only sets the main requirements. Unprotected, the traffic is open to hijacking, impersonation, wiretapping and denial-of-service attacks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fixes the required header orderings for each message type, sets rules for policy, ESP and dynamic keying, and gives example SPD and SAD configurations and step-by-step packet processing.
tldr.outcome: Implementations of the mobile node and home agent must support the formats and rules in Sections 3 and 4. The configuration and processing sections are informative. The RFC was later updated by RFC 4877.

today: RFC 3776 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 4877. It builds on Mobile IPv6 as defined in RFC 3775.

sections.title: Why Mobile IPv6 Needs IPsec
sections.content:
In Mobile IPv6 a mobile node is always reachable at its home address. When it is on a foreign link it also has a care-of address, and it registers the pairing with a router on its home link, the home agent, by sending a Binding Update. The home agent answers with a Binding Acknowledgement.

If this control traffic is unprotected, mobile nodes and correspondent nodes are open to man-in-the-middle, hijacking, passive wiretapping, impersonation and denial-of-service attacks, and third parties can be attacked too. The base specification therefore uses IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) to protect the control traffic. That traffic is Binding Updates and Acknowledgements, the Home Test Init and Home Test messages of return routability that pass through the home agent, and the ICMPv6 messages used for prefix discovery.

The RFC discusses the base requirements in more depth, shows packet formats, describes configuration and shows the order in which packets should be processed. Implementations MUST support at least the formats of Section 3 and obey the rules of Section 4. The configuration and processing sections are informative.
sections.eli5: A traveling device keeps telling its home base where it is. If a stranger could fake those messages, they could steal its mail. IPsec is the lock on the envelope.

sections.title: Required Packet Formats
sections.content:
Section 3 lists, for each kind of message, the headers an implementation MUST support at least, in order. For a Binding Update sent from away from home, the IPv6 header carries the care-of address as source, followed by a Destination Options header holding the Home Address option, an ESP header in transport mode, and the Mobility header holding the Binding Update. The Binding Update also carries an Alternate Care-of Address option, which makes ESP protect the care-of address. The Binding Acknowledgement goes back with a type 2 Routing header carrying the home address, then ESP in transport mode.

When the mobile node is at home, for example to de-register, it can use its home address as the source, and the Home Address option and Routing header are not needed.

Return routability messages (Home Test Init and Home Test) and optional payload packets use ESP in tunnel mode. The outer header uses the care-of address and the home agent, and the inner header uses the home address and the correspondent node. Prefix discovery uses ESP in transport mode, like Binding Updates, around ICMPv6 Mobile Prefix Solicitation and Advertisement messages.

Tunnel-mode packets rely on the mobile node's end of the tunnel changing as it moves. The home agent keeps the same address, but the mobile node's address follows its care-of address.
sections.eli5: Every kind of message has a fixed way of being wrapped, like a letter inside a locked box inside a mailing sleeve. Both sides must wrap in the same order or the other side will not understand.

sections.title: Mandatory Rules for Nodes
sections.content:
Section 4 sets the rules for both mobile nodes and home agents. Manual configuration of security associations MUST be supported; automatic key management with IKE MAY be, and only IKEv1 is discussed. ESP for Binding Updates and Acknowledgements MUST be supported and MUST be used. ESP for Home Test Init, Home Test and prefix discovery messages MUST be supported and SHOULD be used. ESP for payload packets MAY be supported and used. If multicast group membership control protocols or stateful address autoconfiguration protocols are supported, payload protection MUST be supported for them.

For policy matching, a home address in a Home Address option counts as the packet's source address, and a home address in a type 2 Routing header counts as its destination address. Protection of return routability and payload packets MUST be applied only to packets entering the tunnel between the mobile node and the home agent.

Binding Updates and prefix discovery use ESP in transport mode with a non-null authentication algorithm. Return routability uses tunnel mode and needs a non-null encryption transform and a non-null authentication algorithm, which stops an on-link attacker on an unprotected wireless link from seeing both halves of the exchange. The RFC warns that DES, the encryption algorithm mandated by the IPsec standards of that time, is not considered secure, which is especially a problem with manual keys that stay in use for a long time.

A mobile node MUST use the Alternate Care-of Address option in Binding Updates sent while away from home, and MUST use the Home Address option in Binding Updates and Mobile Prefix Solicitations. The home agent MUST use the type 2 Routing header in Binding Acknowledgements and Mobile Prefix Advertisements. When a Binding Update changes the care-of address, the home agent MUST use the new address as the destination of later packets on those tunnel security associations, and it MUST do this only because of Binding Updates protected by IPsec.
sections.eli5: The rules say which messages must be locked, which should be, and which are optional. They also say that only a properly locked note can change where your mail goes.

sections.title: Dynamic Keying with IKE
sections.content:
Anti-replay protection needs dynamic keying. IPsec does not ensure correct ordering of messages, so Mobile IPv6 uses sequence numbers for that. If the 16 bit sequence number space is cycled through, or the home agent reboots and loses its sequence state, replay and reordering attacks become possible. Dynamic keying, IPsec anti-replay protection and the Mobile IPv6 sequence numbers together prevent them.

With IKE version 1 and preshared secrets, main mode picks the secret from the peer's IP address, which may be a care-of address and so does not say which mobile node is calling. For that case aggressive mode MUST be used. Identity choice also matters: with an ID_IPV6_ADDR identity payload, identities cannot be mapped to keys unambiguously.

IKE runs from the care-of address, but the IPsec security associations it creates use home addresses, which are requested as the client identity. The home agent has to verify that a given phase 1 identity is allowed to create security associations for a given home address, so one mobile node cannot send Binding Updates on behalf of another. How that mapping is kept is out of scope, but a locally administered table is one option.

The mobile node and home agent use the Key Management Mobility Capability (K) flag in Binding Updates and Acknowledgements to show whether they can move the IKE endpoints. If they cannot, both sides drop the phase 1 connection made over the old care-of address and set up a new one.
sections.eli5: Some locks need fresh keys each time. This section says how to get those keys even though your address keeps changing, and how to make sure only you can ask for keys tied to your home.

sections.title: Example SPD and SAD Configurations
sections.content:
Section 5 shows Security Policy Database (SPD) and Security Association Database (SAD) entries for an example mobile node with home address home_address_1 and a home agent home_agent_1. Manual configuration gives named security associations, for example SA1 with SPI spi_a in ESP transport mode for Mobility Header traffic from the mobile node and SA2 for the reverse direction.

Return routability entries are matched on the tunnel interface and use ESP tunnel mode. They sit below the Binding Update entries in the ordered SPD, so the Binding Update entries take precedence. The SA from the home agent to the mobile node uses the current care-of address as its destination, which is updated as the node moves.

Prefix discovery entries protect all ICMPv6 traffic between the two nodes, since IPsec may not be able to tell ICMPv6 types apart. Payload entries use a protocol placeholder X and have lower precedence, and X should not be AH or ESP because nested encapsulation is not required by RFC 2401. For MLD and DHCPv6, which may use link-local addresses, the source and destination can be wildcards.

The dynamic keying examples have the same shape but name an IKE phase 1 identity such as user_1 instead of fixed SAs. This makes the home agent configuration user-specific, because every user or home address needs its own entry.
sections.eli5: This is like a sample rule book for a mail room: if a letter comes from this person to that person, use this lock. It shows how to write the rules down so everyone does it the same way.

sections.title: Processing Steps Inside a Node
sections.content:
Section 6 walks through what happens to a packet. For a Binding Update leaving the mobile node, Mobile IPv6 first builds the packet with the home address as source. The Home Address option is added without swapping addresses yet, then ESP is applied, and only just before sending are the addresses swapped so the care-of address becomes the source. This ordering lets IPsec policy lookups see the home address.

The home agent does the reverse. It processes the Home Address option first, then the ESP header, then checks that the result matches the policy for that security association. It then passes the Binding Update on, and updates any return routability or payload security associations with the new care-of address. Binding Acknowledgements are handled the same way with the type 2 Routing header.

Home Test Init is wrapped in a tunnel-mode ESP packet from the care-of address to the home agent, and the home agent unwraps and forwards it. Establishing new security associations begins with IKE phase 1 and phase 2 over the care-of address, then continues like an ordinary Binding Update. During rekeying, Mobility header packets may use the existing security associations, and the new ones should be used as soon as they are available.

Deleting a security association does not have to mean losing a binding. Deletions may happen only to limit active cryptographic contexts, and the RFC says that if more traffic needs to be sent it is preferable to bring up another security association.
sections.eli5: Think of getting dressed: socks before shoes. Here the steps must happen in the right order, or the packet will not make sense to the one who opens it.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations may support other formats than those of Section 3, but the peer may then silently discard the packets unless support has been verified off-line. The tunnel format for return routability and payload packets was chosen because it avoids twenty four bytes of overhead that a Home Address option or Routing header would add, which may matter for real-time traffic. It does require the home agent to change the destination of IPsec packets as the mobile node moves, through an API, by replacing the SA, or by modifying the packet after IPsec processing.

Policy entries specific to a tunnel interface mean implementations must treat the home agent to mobile node tunnel as its own interface for IPsec SPDs. The RFC also notes that IKE with certificates can hit fragmentation: large certificates or chains lead to fragments that many firewalls drop and routers may discard. Mobile IPv6 deployments typically use short certificate chains, and storing peer certificates locally may help.

Bump-in-the-stack (BITS) IPsec implementations face extra work. They must process the Home Address option and type 2 Routing header, detect IPv6 encapsulated traffic, and offer APIs to update SA endpoints.
sections.eli5: Building this is fiddly. A smaller wrapper saves space, but the software has to be able to change the address on the wrapper as you move.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is short. The Mobile IPv6 base specification requires strong security between the mobile node and the home agent, and this memo shows how to arrange it with IPsec. The related security considerations, including the implications of manual versus dynamic keying, are in the base specification.

No IANA actions are needed.
sections.eli5: The big safety discussion lives in the main Mobile IPv6 document. This one is the how-to for the locks.
